summary: A best current practice on how IETF protocols use Ethernet frame formats and IEEE 802 parameters. It sets IANA considerations for assignments under the IANA OUI and provides values for use in documentation. It obsoleted RFC 5342 and has since been replaced by RFC 9542.

eli5.summary: It says how the internet's rule-makers should share and use the number labels that Ethernet gear uses, and which fake ones to use in examples.

questions: which mac addresses to use in documentation
what is the iana oui for ethernet
how are ethernet protocol numbers assigned
subtitle: How the IETF assigns Ethernet and IEEE 802 parameter values for interoperability.

tldr.problem: Ethernet and IEEE 802 protocols require globally unique identifiers (MAC addresses, protocol type codes) so that independent implementations can operate on the same networks. These values must be assigned centrally and published.
tldr.mechanism: IANA holds an Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI 00-00-5E) assigned by IEEE, under which it publishes 48-bit and 64-bit MAC address blocks, Ethernet protocol numbers, and other parameters. The RFC defines assignment procedures and reserves documentation values.
tldr.outcome: The IETF community and implementers can obtain MAC addresses and Ethernet protocol numbers from IANA, enabling interoperable equipment, while documentation examples use reserved ranges to avoid conflicts with real deployments.

today: RFC 7042 is a best current practice and the authoritative guide for IEEE 802 parameter assignments under IANA. It was updated by RFC 9542 in May 2023 to reflect additional changes in assignment policies and documentation values. The IANA OUI 00-00-5E remains the source of officially assigned MAC addresses and protocol numbers for IETF standards.

sections.title: IEEE 802 Parameters and IANA's Role
sections.content:
Ethernet and IEEE 802 networks use Media Access Control (MAC) identifiers (also called MAC addresses) and protocol identifiers to label packets and manage device communication. For example, every network interface card has a 48-bit MAC address, and every packet type (IPv4, IPv6, ARP, etc.) has an Ethertype code.

For these values to work across independent implementations, a central authority must assign them uniquely. The IEEE Registration Authority assigns OUIs (Organizationally Unique Identifiers)—three-octet prefixes—to organizations. The IETF obtained OUI 00-00-5E for use under IANA. This RFC defines how IANA assigns values under that OUI and establishes reserved ranges for documentation and testing so that example configurations do not conflict with real deployed systems.
sections.eli5: Ethernet devices all need a unique address like a house number, and Ethernet packets need a type label like a mail service (first-class, priority, etc.). IANA makes sure no two real devices use the same address, and keeps some made-up addresses just for examples in textbooks.

sections.title: MAC Address Identifiers and Assignments
sections.content:
48-bit MAC addresses are the most common Ethernet interface identifiers. They consist of a 3-octet OUI and 3 additional octets assigned by the OUI holder. Under IANA's OUI, the first 3 octets are always 00-00-5E, and the remaining 3 octets (24 bits) provide 2^24 (16 million) possible addresses. These are split into two groups: multicast addresses (starting 01-00-5E for IPv4 multicast and other uses) and unicast addresses (starting 00-00-5E).

The RFC also covers 64-bit MAC identifiers (EUI-64), which extend a 3-octet OUI with 5 additional octets. IPv6 uses a modified form of EUI-64 to create interface identifiers. The RFC defines which blocks are reserved, assigned to protocols like IPv4 multicast or IPv6, available for new assignments, or reserved for documentation. Assignment must be for standards purposes, must use power-of-two sized blocks starting at aligned boundaries, and must be documented in an RFC or Internet-Draft.
sections.eli5: Think of MAC addresses as street addresses: the first part (OUI) is the town, and the rest is the house number. IANA has lots of house numbers to give out, some are already reserved for special uses (like the mailbox or the fire station), and some are set aside as fake addresses that only appear in textbooks.

sections.title: Ethernet Protocol Type Parameters
sections.content:
Ethertypes are 16-bit codes that identify the type of protocol in an Ethernet frame. Common Ethertypes include 0x0800 for IPv4 and 0x86DD for IPv6. The IEEE Registration Authority assigns most Ethertypes; however, the IETF can use SNAP (Subnetwork Access Protocol) format to create extended protocol identifiers using an OUI plus a 2-byte protocol number. Under the IANA OUI, protocol numbers are assigned using the SNAP format (00-00-5E followed by the 2-byte protocol number).

Additionally, when very large blocks of MAC addresses or protocol numbers are needed—such as 2^17 or more identifiers—or when reserved values are involved, approval requires IESG Ratification rather than just Expert Review. The RFC also assigns documentation protocol numbers (0x0042 under IANA OUI) and documentation MAC addresses so that examples in RFCs do not accidentally collide with real deployments.
sections.eli5: Ethertype numbers tell Ethernet what kind of data is in each packet. IANA can create its own type numbers by combining its OUI with additional bytes, letting it hand out numbers for new protocols without asking IEEE every time.

sections.title: Assignment Procedures and Expert Review
sections.content:
Small to medium assignments of MAC address blocks (up to 2^16 identifiers) go through Expert Review. An applicant completes a template and submits it to IANA, which forwards it to an appointed expert. The expert performs a light sanity check for small blocks, with increased scrutiny for medium-sized ones. If the expert approves and code points are available, IANA makes the assignment.

For large assignments (2^17 or more identifiers) or reserved values, the process requires IESG Ratification. The expert reviews the application as before, but if they recommend approval or believe the IESG should decide, the application goes to the IESG for a management vote. All assignments must be for standards purposes, documented in an RFC or Internet-Draft, and must not circumvent vendors' need to obtain their own IEEE OUI for proprietary use.
sections.eli5: When someone asks for a few address numbers, a volunteer expert just checks that the request makes sense. For very large blocks or special cases, the IETF's steering group has to vote and approve it.

sections.title: Changes and Current Status
sections.content:
RFC 7042 obsoletes RFC 5342 and consolidates documentation on MAC address and protocol assignments. Key improvements include deprecating the 'CF Series' of OUIs (used for PPP) and eliminating requirements for parallel unicast and multicast assignments that proved impractical. The RFC adds Address Family Numbers (AFNs) and DNS Resource Record Types (RRTYPEs) for 48-bit and 64-bit MAC addresses, enabling new ways to query and store MAC address records.

The RFC updates RFC 2153 to deprecate its use of 'CF Series' identifiers and forbid IANA from assigning new values in that series. This consolidation reflects lessons learned from decades of managing Ethernet parameters and ensures clarity on what values are available, what is reserved for documentation, and how to request new assignments going forward.
sections.eli5: This version improved how IANA keeps track of Ethernet numbers, stopped using one old set of fake numbers that were rarely needed, and made it easier to store addresses in databases like DNS.
